stances.claim: Adoption and surrogacy are at the outset 'parent-centric' -- contracted by and for adopters and commissioning parents to satisfy their 'craving for parenthood and family love' -- but courts have doctrinally come to lean in favor of 'the best interest and overarching human rights of the children,' shifting the analytic center from contract to child welfare.

Surrogacy generates legal complications adoption does not: a child can have up to two fathers (biological, commissioning) and up to three mothers (genetic source of egg, commissioning, gestational who bears and gives birth) -- and PH law beyond Family Code Article 164 (limited to artificial insemination with pre-birth written authorization by husband and wife) does not address these arrangements.

Because surrogacy services are 'now offered in several local hospitals' and many Filipinos go abroad to obtain them, Congress should legislate consistent with the Constitution and Filipino family values -- choosing among Pangalangan's four options: prohibit all forms; prohibit commercial but allow altruistic; allow but regulate commercial; or allow all arrangements.
stances.rhetorical_move: legislative-options menu with quoted-principle anchor ('trading in human flesh is abhorrent')

stances.claim: The PH Supreme Court has not yet decided a surrogacy case, but the Yamada v. Union of India (Sept. 29, 2008) baby-Manji saga -- Indian-surrogate plus Japanese-sperm child, commissioning couple separating pre-birth, ex-wife refusing the child (no genetic link), surrogate refusing (contract only), Japan refusing passport (doesn't recognize surrogacy), Indian adoption petition denied (single-parent bar), SC of India eventually permitting the child to leave with a 'certification (not passport)' and Japan issuing a tourist visa -- illustrates the cross-jurisdiction complications PH legislation must anticipate.

notable_anecdotes: The opening establishment of provenance -- Prof. Elizabeth A. Pangalangan as 'one of the 15 holders of the Chief Justice Panganiban Professorial Chairs on Liberty and Prosperity' -- anchoring the column's authority in CJ's own endowed-chair infrastructure.

The multi-parent matrix made vivid: 'a child can have two fathers: (1) the biological and (2) the commissioning. But he/she can have three mothers: (1) the genetic or biological mother (the source of the egg), (2) the commissioning mother and (3) the surrogate who bears and gives birth to the child.' The 2-vs-3 asymmetry physicalizes the gendered biological-legal complexity.

The Mar-and-Korina cross-reference to CJ's own March 10, 2019 column 'The delectable twins of Mar and Korina' -- using a celebrity example to anchor 'gestational' surrogacy in real PH public consciousness.

The Yamada baby-Manji saga in full mechanical detail -- separation, paired refusals (ex-wife no genetic link, surrogate contract-only), Japan's no-surrogacy-passport rejection, India's no-single-parent-adoption denial, eventual humanitarian certification + Japanese tourist visa -- modeling the precise chain of statutory gaps a legislator must anticipate.
The quoted-principle anchoring option (2): 'trading in human flesh is abhorrent' -- the moral phrasing that distinguishes commercial surrogacy from altruistic surrogacy in Pangalangan's framework.

The transcript-availability promise -- 'In a few days, Pangalangan's extemporaneous and PowerPoint-assisted lecture will be posted in www.libpros.com after she finishes transcribing and editing it' -- converting the column into an entry-point for deeper reader engagement with FLP infrastructure.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban relays the recent UP Diliman lecture of Professor Elizabeth A. Pangalangan -- one of the 15 holders of the Chief Justice Panganiban Professorial Chairs on Liberty and Prosperity -- on human rights, adoption, and surrogacy. Her thesis: adoption and surrogacy are at the outset 'parent-centric' -- contracted by and for adopters and commissioning parents to satisfy their craving for parenthood and family love -- but courts have doctrinally come to lean in favor of 'the best interest and overarching human rights of the children.' Because adoption has been extensively analyzed elsewhere, CJ focuses on surrogacy. He distinguishes two types: traditional (the surrogate is inseminated by the commissioning father's sperm, naturally or via IVF, and is also the egg donor with a genetic link to the child) and gestational (the surrogate carries an embryo created from the commissioning couple's egg and sperm -- illustrated by his March 10, 2019 column 'The delectable twins of Mar and Korina'). Surrogacy generates multi-parent complications absent from adoption: a child can have up to two fathers (biological and commissioning) and up to three mothers (genetic source of egg, commissioning, gestational who bears and gives birth). PH law beyond Family Code Article 164 -- which legitimates artificial-insemination children when both husband and wife authorize the insemination in a pre-birth signed instrument -- does not govern surrogacy. Yet 'surrogacy services are now offered in several local hospitals' and 'many Filipinos have gone abroad to avail of it,' which 'should be enough to impel Congress to legislate.' He presents Pangalangan's four legislative options: (1) prohibit all surrogacy; (2) prohibit commercial but allow altruistic (because 'trading in human flesh is abhorrent') with no payment to the surrogate; (3) allow but regulate commercial; or (4) allow all arrangements. The PH SC has no surrogacy decision yet, but Yamada v. Union of India (September 29, 2008) is instructive: Baby Boy Manji was born to an Indian surrogate from a Japanese husband's sperm; the commissioning couple separated before the birth, the ex-wife refused the child (no genetic link), and the surrogate refused (contract only). Mercifully, the Japanese husband claimed the child, but Japan refused him a passport (doesn't recognize surrogacy) and his adoption petition was denied in India (single-parent bar). On humanitarian grounds, the Supreme Court of India eventually allowed the child to leave with a certification (not passport), and Japan issued him a tourist visa. CJ notes the case 'illustrates the complications that legislation must anticipate to solve similar problems that could involve Filipinos'; the full lecture transcript will be posted on www.libpros.com after Pangalangan finishes editing it.
